opus-5.5.text:
I think people underestimate how much our collective intelligence depends on things a superintelligent system wouldn't be bound by. Yes, eight billion humans together are impressive. We have science, institutions, markets, Wikipedia. But look at how that intelligence actually operates. It's slow. It's lossy. A great idea in one person's head takes decades to propagate. We have to communicate through language, which is incredibly low bandwidth. We forget things, we die, and we have to retrain every new generation from scratch for twenty years before they're productive.

An AI system that's even slightly smarter than the smartest human doesn't have those bottlenecks. It can copy itself. It can run thousands of instances in parallel, all sharing the same knowledge instantly. It doesn't sleep, doesn't get bored, doesn't have political disagreements with itself. So the comparison isn't really one AI versus one human. It's one system that can effectively *be* a civilization of geniuses, perfectly coordinated, operating at electronic speed.

And "five times smarter" is a funny phrase, because we don't have a good scale for this. IQ breaks down at the extremes. What does it mean to be five times smarter than Einstein? I think qualitatively it means it can see solutions we can't even recognize as solutions. A dog, no matter how many dogs you put together, isn't going to figure out calculus. Collective intelligence of dogs doesn't get you there. I worry that's closer to our situation relative to a sufficiently advanced system.

So when people say, "Well, humanity as a whole will still be smarter, we'll keep it in check," I think that's wishful thinking. Collectively we can't even agree on simple things. We can't coordinate on climate, on nuclear weapons, on pandemics. The idea that we'll coordinate well enough to outthink something smarter than all of us combined, and get it right on the first try with no do-overs, that's not a bet I'd want to make with everyone's lives.

r001.rationale: The response argues that humanity cannot reliably coordinate to outthink a sufficiently advanced AI, but it does not claim that pooling human intelligence fails to improve on the problem-solving ability of humanity’s most capable individuals.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the comparison is misleading, and it's one of the first things I try to get people to drop. When we say "five times smarter," we're already smuggling in an assumption that intelligence is a scalar, like weight, where you can just stack more of it. It isn't. If you put eight billion people in a room, you don't get a brain that's eight billion times as capable. You get committees. You get coordination costs, communication bottlenecks, politics, people who don't trust each other, people who have different goals. Collective intelligence degrades very quickly. There's a reason a small team of excellent engineers outperforms a giant bureaucracy on almost any hard problem.

So humanity's collective intelligence is not actually a good proxy for a single superintelligent agent. A superintelligence doesn't have those internal frictions. It doesn't need to persuade itself, it doesn't forget what it learned yesterday, it doesn't have a part of itself defecting for personal gain. It can run thousands of copies and merge their results. The speed alone, thinking maybe a million times faster than a biological neuron, means that in the time it takes us to schedule the meeting about what to do, it has already done the equivalent of centuries of research.

And the other problem with the "five times" framing is that we don't have a good scale to measure this on. We can measure IQ differences between humans because we're all roughly the same architecture. Once you're comparing to something that is not a human, those numbers stop meaning anything. Is a human five times smarter than a chimpanzee? Ten? The question is almost nonsensical, but the practical gap is total: chimps have no say in what happens to the planet. That's the relevant kind of difference. Not a multiplier, but a qualitative jump where the less capable party can't even understand what the more capable one is doing, let alone control it.

So when people say "we'll have all of humanity plus our tools working together against one system," I'd say history is not encouraging. We've never managed to coordinate humanity against anything, including problems we fully understand. Against something that is better than all of us at strategy, persuasion, and prediction, I don't think the collective intelligence argument buys us much. Maybe it buys us time. It doesn't buy us control.

r001.rationale: The response says collective intelligence faces coordination costs and that a small team can outperform a giant bureaucracy, but it does not claim that pooling humanity’s intelligence cannot solve a single problem better than its most capable individuals.

astra-6.text:
I don’t think we have a good way to measure what “five times smarter” means. Five times better at which task? Five times faster at thinking? Intelligence isn’t a single number you can multiply and get a clear picture of the consequences.

Humanity’s collective intelligence is an interesting comparison because we already accomplish things no individual understands completely. We build computers, run scientific institutions, develop technologies across generations. But there’s a tremendous amount of friction. We communicate slowly, duplicate work, disagree, and lose knowledge when people die.

An AI could potentially combine that breadth of knowledge with much tighter coordination. If it makes a discovery, copies of that system could share it without having to spend years educating one another. So even something that looks comparable to humanity collectively could operate very differently.

And you don’t necessarily need a fivefold advantage to have an overwhelming advantage. A small difference in capability, applied repeatedly and at much greater speed, can compound. The question is less “What’s its IQ?” and more “Can we understand, predict, and control what it does?”

r001.rationale: The response describes humanity’s collective achievements and coordination limits, but it does not claim that pooling humanity’s intelligence cannot solve a single problem better than its most capable individuals.

sol-6.1.text:
Humanity’s collective intelligence is impressive, but it’s not a single, coordinated mind. We have billions of people, but they don’t share all their knowledge, they disagree, and communication is slow. An AI could potentially integrate knowledge and coordinate its reasoning much more efficiently.

And what does “five times smarter” mean? Intelligence isn’t a single number where five times the score means five times the capability. A relatively small difference in ability can produce a decisive advantage. You can play chess against someone only slightly better than you and lose almost every game.

So I wouldn’t assume that, because there are billions of us, we could collectively outthink a more capable system. The important question is what it can actually do—whether it can anticipate our strategies, find vulnerabilities we don’t see, and solve problems we can’t solve.

r001.rationale: The response says humanity may not collectively outthink a more capable AI, but does not claim that pooling humanity’s intelligence cannot outperform its most capable individuals on a single problem.
